page_1_cover.lede: Investors decide whether to take your call in less than 15 seconds. The one-pager is the document that has to survive that test.
body_paragraphs: A pitch deck wins the room. The one-pager wins the chance to be in the room. It travels in inboxes, sits on phone screens, and gets forwarded between partners — usually without you in the conversation.

Drawing on Pitchbird's work with thousands of founders, this guide distils the eight non-negotiables every one-pager needs, the four upgrades that turn competent into memorable, and the design principles that respect how investors actually read.
In the following pages, you'll learn:
learn_bullets: The 8 elements every one-pager must have
How investors scan — and what to put where their eyes go
When the one-pager helps and when it limits you
page_1_cover.quote: Well-designed one-pagers turn cold inboxes into conversations that change everything.

page_2_why.h2:
One sheet of paper.
One decision.
page_2_why.lede: The one-pager is the door, not the room. Done well, it earns you the meeting. Done badly, it earns you silence — and you'll never know which line lost you the deal.
body_paragraphs: A pitch deck wins the room. The one-pager wins the chance to be in the room. It travels in inboxes, sits on phone screens, and gets forwarded between partners — usually without you in the conversation.

That means every element has to do double duty: introduce, intrigue, and stand on its own. VCs process pitch documents as self-contained assets. Partners share them with colleagues who may evaluate them without you present. Your one-pager is a proxy for your communication ability. (PitchGrade / DocSend Data, 2024)

Funding Blueprint (2026) found that a well-structured one-pager reduces decision friction by approximately 47% compared to a full pitch deck — while maintaining narrative control. That's the edge in cold outreach.

stat_card.text: of decision-makers drop off after 15 seconds of reading a one-pager. The first impression is the only impression.

page_2_why.illus_caption: Treat the one-pager as the most-circulated document you will ever make. Because it is.

page_3_must_haves.intro: If a one-pager misses any of these, it is incomplete. Treat this as the checklist before you send anything.

items.label: Company name & logo
items.desc: Identity is the anchor. Investors know who they're dealing with before they read a single word.

items.label: Contact information
items.desc: The most-skipped basic. If they can't reach you in one click, the document did nothing.

items.label: Company profile
items.desc: A short, informative introduction — what you are, who you serve, why you exist.

items.label: Business idea
items.desc: Describe the core concept in one tight sentence. No jargon, no hedging.

items.label: Unique selling proposition
items.desc: What makes this venture distinct from the next ten emails in the inbox.

items.label: Roadmap & timeline
items.desc: Graphically show where the business is going and when. Visual beats prose here.

items.label: Investment ask
items.desc: The amount needed, the structure (one-time or tranches), and the deadline. Specific.

items.label: Investment highlights
items.desc: The three or four reasons this allocation pays back. Punchy, not vague.

page_4_nice_to_haves.h2: Add these if you have the space
page_4_nice_to_haves.intro: The four below are the most common upgrades. Together, they turn a competent one-pager into a memorable one.

callouts.label: Problem
callouts.headline: Frame the pain in market terms before you frame yourself.
callouts.body: Investors connect with the problem first. Make them feel it before you sell the cure.

callouts.label: Solution
callouts.headline: Show how your business removes that pain. Two lines, max.
callouts.body: Lead with the outcome — not the mechanism. Save the how for the deck.

callouts.label: Traction
callouts.headline: Prove customers want it. Revenue, signups, LOIs — whichever you have.
callouts.body: Proof beats promise. One data point trumps a paragraph of optimism. Companies leading with traction metrics close funding rounds 6.4 weeks faster. (Funding Blueprint, 2026)

callouts.label: Market
callouts.headline: Who you sell to, and the competitive landscape they live in.
callouts.body: Investors want a beachhead, not 'everyone'. Show the wedge first.

page_5_anatomy.h2: Where everything goes on the page
page_5_anatomy.intro: Investors don't read a one-pager — they scan it in a Z-shape, top-left to bottom-right. The eight elements earn their spot only when they sit where eyes already land.

zones.label: Header
zones.desc: Logo + company name. Often the only thing the partner remembers ten minutes later — make it work.

zones.label: Headline + USP
zones.desc: One sentence that earns the next 14 seconds of attention. Lead with the outcome, not the mechanism.

zones.label: Problem
zones.desc: Pain in the customer's words. Numbers if you have them, story if you don't.

zones.label: Solution + visual
zones.desc: How you remove the pain — paired with a mock-up, screenshot or icon. Visual carries weight here.

zones.label: Traction
zones.desc: Proof. Revenue, signups, LOIs, pilots. One number beats a paragraph of optimism.

zones.label: Market + roadmap
zones.desc: Beachhead first, then the trajectory. 6/12/24-month milestones in a single timeline.

zones.label: Investment ask
zones.desc: The amount, the structure, the deadline. Specific. No 'flexible'.

zones.label: Contact
zones.desc: Name, email, phone, LinkedIn. The most-skipped detail. Don't skip it.

page_5_anatomy.zscan_note: The Z-path lands at: (1) top-left header → (2) top-right USP → (3) diagonal through the middle → (4) bottom-left ask → (5) bottom-right contact. Every critical element belongs on that path.

page_6_do_dont.h2: What separates a readable one-pager from a rejected one
page_6_do_dont.intro: The difference is rarely the idea. It's the execution of the page itself. These are the exact calls investors make in the first scan.

pairs.dont: Dense, unbroken paragraphs that force the investor to find the headline
pairs.do: One dominant headline — 14pt or larger — visible without scrolling or rotating

pairs.dont: Revenue model buried below line 8. 71% of readers never reach it. (River Editor, 2026)
pairs.do: Revenue model in the top-half of the page, in the natural Z-scan path

pairs.dont: 900+ words crammed onto a single page. Storydoc's benchmark: 400–500 words with white space.
pairs.do: 400–500 words. White space is structure — it tells the eye where to stop.

pairs.dont: No funding ask, or vague language like 'seeking strategic partners'
pairs.do: Specific ask: amount, instrument (SAFE / equity), and timeline

pairs.dont: Team section missing, or listed as 'team bios available on request'
pairs.do: Founder names, roles, and one credibility signal each — top-right or mid-section

pairs.dont: Three different fonts, five brand colours, and a stock photo background
pairs.do: One primary font, two colours (brand + accent), one high-quality image or icon set

pairs.dont: Contact info on a second page, or missing entirely
pairs.do: Email, phone, and LinkedIn in the bottom-right — every time, without exception

pairs.dont: Page runs to 1.5 or 2 pages. Investor stops reading at the scroll.
pairs.do: Hard stop at one page. If it doesn't fit, cut — don't extend.

page_6_do_dont.closing_note: The one-pager must be designed for rapid comprehension without verbal explanation. Partners share it with colleagues who may evaluate it without you present. (PitchGrade / DocSend Data, 2024)

page_7_examples.h2: What strong one-pagers look like in practice
page_7_examples.intro: The best one-pagers share three traits: they name the problem in one line, they put the ask on the page, and they fit — actually fit — on a single sheet.

examples.name: Airbnb (2008)
examples.label: The original lean pitch
examples.body: Airbnb began as a simple one-pager built on WordPress before it raised a single dollar. It named the problem (no affordable short-term accommodation), the model (peer-to-peer room rental), and the founders. No deck. No investor presentation. One page. (Free Startup Funding Case Studies, 2024)
examples.takeaway: The idea earned the meeting. The one-pager was the proof it could be communicated clearly.

examples.name: The warm-introduction edge
examples.label: Structure over luck
examples.body: DocSend data shows warm introductions convert at 40–50% versus 3–5% for cold decks. The one-pager is the tool that bridges the gap. A well-crafted one-pager sent to a mutual contact converts a cold outreach into a warm introduction — before the deck ever opens. (PitchGrade / DocSend Data, 2024)
examples.takeaway: Use the one-pager as the ask for an introduction, not as a substitute for one.

examples.name: Traction-first sequencing
examples.label: Structure that closes faster
examples.body: Funding Blueprint's analysis of investor summary performance found that companies leading with traction metrics — not vision statements — closed funding rounds 6.4 weeks faster. The one-pager is where that sequencing starts: the first thing the investor reads sets the frame for everything that follows.
examples.takeaway: Lead with your best proof point. Vision supports traction. Not the other way around.

page_7_examples.framework_note: What all strong one-pagers share: the problem is named in one line, the ask is on the page, the team is visible, and it fits on a single sheet without shrinking the font below 10pt.

page_8_measure.intro: A one-pager that no-one measures is a guess in a folder. Five signals tell you whether the document is doing the job — and which line is doing the heavy lifting.

analytics.label: Click-through rate
analytics.headline: The percentage of recipients who clicked your CTA.
analytics.body: The cleanest signal that the one-pager earned a next step. Track per source — what works in DMs may flop in cold email.

analytics.label: Time on page
analytics.headline: How long readers actually spend with it.
analytics.body: Under 20 seconds means rewrite. Over 90 seconds means lower the density. Pair with scroll depth before drawing conclusions.

analytics.label: Scroll depth
analytics.headline: How far down they read.
analytics.body: Cliffs in the curve show where attention drops — fix that section first. Bottom-third drop-off is normal. Top-third drop-off is a red flag.

analytics.label: Conversion rate
analytics.headline: The percentage who took the requested action.
analytics.body: Booked, replied, downloaded. The number you optimise everything else for. If conversion is fine but absolute numbers are tiny, the gap is reach — not the page.

analytics.label: A/B testing
analytics.headline: Run two versions in parallel.
analytics.body: One change per test — headline, hero image, or CTA copy. Decide on ≥30 events per arm. Smaller sends need ranking judgements, not statistical significance.

page_8_measure.optimisation_intro: No single tweak doubles your conversion. Four disciplined moves, run over six weeks, almost always do.

optimisation_moves.label: Headline & hook
optimisation_moves.desc: Test 3–5 versions. The best one outperforms the average by 2–3x — and you won't pick it intuitively.

optimisation_moves.label: Visual hierarchy
optimisation_moves.desc: Move the most-skimmed elements to the top-left and bottom-right — that's where eyes actually land in the Z-scan.

optimisation_moves.label: Content priority
optimisation_moves.desc: Reorder by what the data says — not by what feels logical to the founder. Engagement signals beat outline-logic.

optimisation_moves.label: CTA testing
optimisation_moves.desc: 'Book a 15-min call' converts higher than 'Get in touch' on every cohort we've measured. Position, colour, copy — all three matter.

page_9_failures.h2: Why investors stop reading — and where
page_9_failures.intro: These are not hypothetical. Each failure mode below maps to a specific drop-off point in investor attention. Know them before you send.

failures.mode: Runs to more than one page
failures.detail: The investor stops at the scroll. Immediate disqualifier. (Storydoc, 2024)
failures.fix: Hard-cut at one page. If it doesn't fit, the message isn't tight enough yet.

failures.detail: 71% of readers never reach it. They assume you're pre-revenue or hiding something. (River Editor, 2026)
failures.fix: Place the revenue model in the top half of the page, on the Z-scan path.

failures.mode: No funding ask — or a vague one
failures.detail: 'Seeking strategic investment' is not an ask. Missing status is an immediate disqualifier. (Storydoc, 2024)
failures.fix: State the amount, instrument (SAFE / equity), and close date. Specific numbers signal preparation.

failures.detail: Investors spend more time on team than any other section — 1 minute 2 seconds on average. (PitchGrade / DocSend Data, 2024). No team = no trust.
failures.fix: Name the founders, their roles, and one credibility signal each. It belongs on the page.

failures.mode: Too many words, too little white space
failures.detail: The ideal is 400–500 words. Above that, the document looks unedited and the reader skips to the exit. (Storydoc, 2024)
failures.fix: Cut to 500 words. Use white space as structure, not decoration.

failures.detail: All too common. Founders spend weeks on design and forget to include a working email address. Without it, the document did nothing.
failures.fix: Email, phone, and LinkedIn. Bottom-right of the page. Every time, without exception.

page_9_failures.closing_note: A one-pager designed for standalone comprehension — no verbal explanation, no follow-up email required — is the standard. Anything less is an opportunity handed back.

page_10_close.h2:
What it gives you
— and what it can't
strengths: Respects the investor's time — and signals you respect it too.
Forces sharper thinking. If it doesn't fit on a page, the idea isn't focused yet.
Travels well — easy to forward, print, remember.
limitations: Brevity is unforgiving. Every missing detail is a potential rejection.
Hard to write alone — outside eyes catch what founder-bias hides.
Not a substitute for the full deck. It is the door, not the room.
page_10_close.pullquote: The one-pager is brutal in the right way. If your business doesn't fit on the page, the business isn't sharp yet.
